sections.h2: What should I know before selling a house fast in Edwardsville, IL?
sections.html:
Edwardsville sellers are working in a college and commuter town of about 26,500 people where Census figures for 2020 to 2024 put the middle owner-occupied home at $299,800. Speed depends mostly on three things: the condition of the house, how clean the title is, and how soon the Madison County paperwork can be assembled.

Most sales follow one of three routes. One path is an agent listing with showings, another is a sale by owner, and a third is an as-is cash purchase with a closing date you pick. A cash sale removes repairs and showings from the process. Recording, transfer tax and property tax questions stay the same on every route, so the sections below cover those first.

  • Gather the parcel number (PIN) from your Madison County tax bill.
  • Find your mortgage payoff figure and any liens on the property.
  • Check whether tenants occupy the home, because the city tracks rentals by registration.
  • Decide whether you want a closing within weeks or a longer marketing period.

sections.h2: What is Edwardsville like for a home seller?
sections.html:
Madison County's seat is Edwardsville, a city in the Metro East region, roughly 18 miles northeast of downtown St. Louis. About 19.81 square miles of land make up the city, and the 2020 Census counted 26,808 residents. The Census Bureau estimated 26,463 for July 1, 2025, a 1.4 percent dip from the April 2020 base.

The city was incorporated in 1818 and named for Ninian Edwards. Southern Illinois University Edwardsville and the headquarters of Prairie Farms Dairy anchor the local economy, which explains the young population: the 2020 median age was 30.1. The Leclaire neighborhood, built by a plumbing manufacturer in the 1890s and folded into the city in 1934, is a National Register historic district. Saint Louis Street, listed in 1983, holds more than 50 homes from the mid 1800s and early 1900s.

Buyers here weigh school boundaries heavily. Most of the city belongs to Edwardsville Community Unit School District 7, while small slivers fall within Granite City CUSD 9, Wood River-Hartford Elementary District 15 and East Alton-Wood River Community High School District 14. Confirm the district for a specific address before you advertise it.

sections.h2: What do Census figures say about Edwardsville housing?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau reports 9,828 households in Edwardsville and a 66.6 percent owner-occupied rate for 2020 to 2024. Median gross rent was $1,306, and the median household income was $86,721. The 2020 count showed 10,456 housing units with a rental vacancy rate of 14.2 percent, a figure worth knowing if you own a rental, since tenants have choices.

A median is only a midpoint. A house on Saint Louis Street, a 1990s subdivision home and a rental near campus can sit far apart on price, so base your asking figure on closed sales of similar houses nearby.

sections.h2: How do weather and tornado history affect a house in Edwardsville?
sections.html:
Madison County has real storm exposure. A tornado outbreak on December 10 and 11, 2021 hit Edwardsville hard, and an EF3 tornado collapsed an Amazon warehouse in the city. Buyers and insurers often ask about roof age, window condition and any past storm repairs, so keep receipts and permit records handy.

The local climate swings widely. Average temperatures run from a January low near 19 degrees Fahrenheit to a July high near 90, with a record low of minus 27 in January 1977 and a record high of 114 in July 2012. Edwardsville falls in Climate Zone 4A under the International Energy Conservation Code. Heating and cooling equipment therefore gets a real workout, and an old furnace or failing air conditioner will come up in any inspection.

If storm damage is still unrepaired, a buyer who purchases as-is can take the house in that condition, which is one reason sellers with damaged roofs or water-stained ceilings look at cash offers.

sections.h2: What rental rules apply if I own a rental house in Edwardsville?
sections.html:
Edwardsville runs a Rental Registration and Inspection Program, and owners must register each rental property every year. The 2026 form lists a $40 annual fee for a single-family or mobile home building, $60 for a duplex, and $25 per unit for buildings with three or more units. A registration received after January 31 carries a $75 late fee, and a first re-inspection is free while later ones cost $75.

Ownership changes matter at closing. The form says a change in ownership requires deregistration, and its checkbox reasons include Property Sold. A new owner must register within 30 days of taking ownership, and the city will not register a property if the owner has unpaid fees or fines. Questions go to rentalregistration@cityofedwardsville.com or 618-307-1501.

  • Deregister the property after the sale so city records show you are no longer the owner.
  • Clear any outstanding city fees or fines before closing.
  • Tell the buyer whether the unit has tenants, since the city expects inspections before occupancy.
  • Smoke detectors belong in each sleeping room, within 15 feet of sleeping rooms and on each level, with carbon monoxide detectors within 15 feet of sleeping rooms.

sections.h2: How do recording and transfer tax work for an Edwardsville sale?
sections.html:
Deeds for Edwardsville property are recorded with the Madison County Recorder. The Recorder states that the State of Illinois collects $.50 per $500 of taxable consideration, or part thereof, and Madison County collects $.25 per $500, or part thereof. Every deed needs a Real Estate Transfer Declaration (PTAX) or a statement of exemption, and the county page lists the exemptions under 35 ILCS 200/31-45.

The recorder also asks for a few items that trip up self-managed closings. Deeds must carry the grantee's name and address for tax billing, and a notarized Plat Act affidavit travels with each deed. The permanent parcel number must appear on documents affecting a transfer. The instrument must show who prepared it, and when a deed with money changing hands is paid by check, the recording fee and the transfer tax go in separate checks. A title company or attorney normally handles all of this.

Ask the Recorder's office what the current recording fee is, since the page describing documents does not print a dollar amount.

sections.h2: When are Madison County property taxes due, and what happens at closing?
sections.html:
The county Treasurer collects real estate tax in four installments. For 2025 taxes payable in 2026, the due dates were July 9, September 9, October 9 and December 9. A penalty of 1.5 percent applies to an installment for every 30 days after its due date, and the Treasurer notes that failing to receive a bill does not cancel the liability under 35 ILCS 200/20-15.

Because taxes are billed after the year they cover, the closing statement normally divides the bill between buyer and seller. Your title company or attorney prepares that split, so ask for it in writing before closing day. Unpaid taxes are sold at the annual tax sale, and the owner may redeem for up to two to three years, but a lien like that complicates a sale and is best cleared first.

If you think the assessment is wrong, the Madison County Board of Review accepts an appeal within 30 days after assessments are published. The Treasurer lists homestead, senior homestead, disabled veterans, returning veterans, disabled persons and senior freeze exemptions. Call the Chief County Assessment Office for the current amounts that apply to your parcel.

sections.h2: Should I gather permit records before selling in Edwardsville?
sections.html:
Work you did to the house needs paperwork, and buyers will ask for it. Edwardsville's building permit application covers new construction, remodeling, garages, roofs, electrical, plumbing and mechanical work, and it has a line that asks whether the property is a rental. Roofing needs an Illinois roofing license number on the form.

Open permits and unpermitted additions can slow a closing, because buyers' lenders and title companies ask about them. Before listing, gather permit records for decks, finished basements, water heaters and furnaces. Ask the city whether any permit on your address remains open, and finish or close it out before you sign a contract.

faqs.q: What if tenants live in my Edwardsville house?
faqs.a: A sale is still possible. The city requires owners to register rentals each year and to deregister when the property sells, so file the Property Sold deregistration after closing. The buyer must register within 30 days of taking ownership. Read the lease and any deposit terms with your closing agent.

faqs.q: What transfer taxes will I owe on an Edwardsville home sale?
faqs.a: The Madison County Recorder lists $.50 per $500 for the State of Illinois and $.25 per $500 for the county, each applied to taxable consideration or part thereof. Your closing agent works out the exact figure from the PTAX declaration. Ask the title company to show the numbers on the settlement statement.

faqs.q: Who handles recording the deed in Edwardsville?
faqs.a: The Madison County Recorder records deeds. A deed needs the PTAX declaration or exemption statement, a notarized Plat Act affidavit, the parcel number and the grantee's tax billing address. Title companies normally submit these on your behalf.

faqs.q: How often are Madison County property taxes billed?
faqs.a: Four times a year. The 2026 schedule listed July 9, September 9, October 9 and December 9. Late installments add 1.5 percent for each 30 days. Check the Treasurer's website for the schedule on your parcel and for proof of what has been paid.

faqs.q: Is a cash sale faster than listing a house in Edwardsville?
faqs.a: Often it is, because there is no marketing period, buyer financing or repair negotiation. The county paperwork, payoff and title steps still apply, so a clean title is what sets the real pace. Get a written payoff and confirm no liens before you accept any offer.
